fact_or_definition_blocks: [L6] Every finite-dimensional endomorphism over an algebraically closed field has Jordan canonical form ([[cor-endomorphisms-over-an-algebraically-closed-field-have-jordan-form]]).
associated_step_blocks: 1.3 Over $\mathbb C$, fix $x\in[\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h]$. By [L6], choose a Jordan basis on $V$ and write $x=x_s+x_n$, where $x_s$ is diagonal, $x_n$ is block-nilpotent, and they commute. The commuting left and right multiplication operators on $\operatorname{End}(V)$ show that the semisimple part of $\operatorname{ad}_x=L_x-R_x$ is $\operatorname{ad}_{x_s}$. Write the diagonal entries of $x_s$ as $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, and let $\overline{x_s}$ have diagonal entries $\overline{a_1},\ldots, \overline{a_n}$. On the generalized eigenspaces of $\operatorname{ad}_x$, $\operatorname{ad}_{\overline{x_s}}$ has eigenvalues $\overline{a_i-a_j}$. Finite Hermite interpolation on the finitely many differences $a_i-a_j$, taking zero to zero, expresses $\operatorname{ad}_{\overline{x_s}}$ as a polynomial without constant term in $\operatorname{ad}_x$. Since $\mathfrak h$ is stable under $\operatorname{ad}_x$, it follows that $[\overline{x_s},\mathfrak h]\subseteq\mathfrak h$. [L6, algebra]

fact_or_definition_blocks: [F6] *Triangularisation of solvable representations.* A finite-dimensional module over a finite-dimensional solvable Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero has a complete invariant flag ([[cor-simultaneous-upper-triangularization-of-solvable-lie-algebra-representations]]).
associated_step_blocks: 2.2 Let $\mathfrak r=\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak g)$ be the radical and choose by [F6] a basis of $W$ in which every $A\in\mathfrak r$ is upper triangular, with diagonal linear forms $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N\in\mathfrak r^*$. The radical is characteristic by [F7], so conjugation by $h\in G$ preserves $\mathfrak r$ and carries the representation $\mathfrak r\to\operatorname{End}(W)$ to an equivalent one; the multiset of diagonal values of the conjugate of $A$ is $\{\lambda_j(A)\}_j$, so each composition $\lambda_i\circ\operatorname{Ad}(h)$ is one of $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N$ (a value function not among them is separated from all of them by evaluating at some $A$ outside finitely many proper hyperplanes). Each map $h\mapsto\lambda_i\circ\operatorname{Ad}(h)$ is a morphism from the connected group $G$ to the finite set $\{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N\}$, hence is constant; differentiating at the identity gives $\lambda_i([X,A])=0$ for all $X\in\mathfrak g$, $A\in\mathfrak r$. Consequently the commutator ideal $\mathfrak n=[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak r]$ is a $\operatorname{Ad}(G)$-stable Lie ideal of $\mathfrak g$ whose elements are strictly upper triangular in this basis. [F6, F7, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $N=\langle\exp(\mathfrak n)\rangle$ and let $U=\overline N$ be its Zariski closure. Every $\exp(tA)$ with $A\in\mathfrak n$ strictly upper triangular is a polynomial function of $t$, so $U$ is a closed connected subgroup of $G$ contained in the upper unitriangular group; it is normal, because $\operatorname{Ad}(G)\mathfrak n=\mathfrak n$ and conjugation commutes with the exponential. To check unipotence in the fixed-vector sense of the definition, let $M$ be a non-zero finite-dimensional rational $U$-module: its Lie algebra $\mathfrak u$ is solvable, so [F6] gives a complete $\mathfrak u$-invariant flag, which by step 2.1 is $U$-invariant, and every diagonal character of $U$ is trivial because on each $\exp(tA)$ it restricts to an algebraic homomorphism $\mathbb C\to\mathbb C^\times$ whose coordinate function and inverse are both polynomial, hence constant; the first line of the flag is therefore a non-zero fixed vector. If $\mathfrak n\neq0$ then $U\neq1$, since the matrix exponential is injective on nilpotent matrices, and reductivity of $G$ forces $\mathfrak n=0$. [F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2]

9.1 The converse recorded in the definition also holds, without using the omitted compact-existence direction. If every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module is completely reducible and $U\subseteq G$ is a closed normal unipotent subgroup, take a faithful finite-dimensional module $W$ from [F2] and a simple submodule $S\subseteq W$; by the fixed-vector definition of unipotence $S^U\neq0$, and $S^U$ is $G$-stable because $U$ is normal, so $S^U=S$ by simplicity and $U$ fixes every simple summand of $W$, hence all of $W$; faithfulness forces $U=1$. Thus linearly reductive implies reductive. Closed subgroups of a fixed-vector unipotent group $U$ are again unipotent, as follows. A faithful finite-dimensional module for $U$ from [F2] has a complete flag with trivial successive characters, by iterating the fixed-vector condition on its quotients, so $U$ is a closed subgroup of an upper unitriangular matrix group. For a closed subgroup $H\subseteq U$ and $h\in H$, the nilpotent matrix $\log h$ is a finite polynomial in $h-1$ and $t\mapsto\exp(t\log h)$ is polynomial. Every defining equation of $H$ vanishes on this curve at all nonnegative integers because these values are $h^n$, so it vanishes identically; the curve lies in $H$ and joins $1$ to $h$. Thus $H$ is connected. The Lie algebra of $H$ is strictly upper triangular, hence solvable. For any nonzero rational $H$-module, [F6] gives a Lie-invariant complete flag, which is $H$-invariant by step 2.1. Its diagonal characters are trivial on each curve $\exp(t\log h)$: an algebraic homomorphism $\mathbb G_a\to\mathbb G_m$ has polynomial coordinate and polynomial inverse, so is constant. Since every $h\in H$ lies on such a curve, the first flag line is fixed by $H$, proving the hereditary assertion. For the identity-component reductions: $G$ is reductive if and only if $G^\circ$ is by the conjugate-product argument of step 7.1 in one direction. For the other direction, if $G^\circ$ is reductive and $U$ is a normal unipotent subgroup of $G$, then $U\cap G^\circ=1$, so $U$ embeds in the finite group $G/G^\circ$. A nontrivial finite group over $\mathbb C$ is not unipotent: its regular representation has the nonzero augmentation submodule, on which the only possible invariant vectors are multiples of the sum of all basis vectors, and none has augmentation zero in characteristic zero. Hence $U=1$; $G$ is linearly reductive if and only if $G^\circ$ is, the forward direction by the implication linearly reductive $G\Rightarrow$ reductive $G\Rightarrow$ reductive $G^\circ$ proved above, followed by step 6.1 and the reverse by the finite averaging of step 7.1. Moreover smoothness makes the irreducible components of $G$ disjoint, so they are the connected components and the cosets of $G^\circ$; there are finitely many of them. [F2, F3, F6, step 2.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1]

fact_or_definition_blocks: [L1] Every finite-dimensional representation of a solvable algebra over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field is simultaneously upper triangularizable ([[cor-simultaneous-upper-triangularization-of-solvable-lie-algebra-representations]]).
associated_step_blocks: 1.1 Suppose first that $\mathfrak h$ is solvable. Choose bases of $\mathfrak h$ and $V$, and let $k_0\subseteq k$ be the subfield generated over $\mathbb Q$ by the finitely many structure constants and matrix entries. The resulting $k_0$-form $\mathfrak h_0$ is solvable because its derived series becomes that of $\mathfrak h$ after the faithful scalar extension $k_0\subseteq k$. The finitely generated field $k_0$ embeds in $\mathbb C$. Over $\mathbb C$, [L1] gives a basis in which $\mathfrak h_0$ is upper triangular and its derived algebra is strictly upper triangular. Thus $\operatorname{tr}(yx)=0$ for all $x\in[\mathfrak h_0,\mathfrak h_0]$ and $y\in\mathfrak h_0$. These finitely many bilinear identities hold over $k_0$ and hence after extension to $k$. [L1, L5, algebra]

fact_or_definition_blocks: [L1] A solvable representation under these field hypotheses is simultaneously upper triangularizable ([[cor-simultaneous-upper-triangularization-of-solvable-lie-algebra-representations]]).
associated_step_blocks: 1.1 Suppose first that $n=\dim V>0$. By [L1], choose a basis of $V$ in which every element of $\mathfrak g$ is upper triangular. The diagonal of $AB-BA$ is zero for upper triangular $A,B$, so every bracket is strictly upper triangular. Since strictly upper triangular matrices form a linear subspace, every element of $[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]$, which is a finite linear combination of brackets, is strictly upper triangular and therefore has its $n$th power zero. [given, L1, algebra]

fact_or_definition_blocks: [L1] Hermitian positive-definite matrices and Cholesky factorisations with positive diagonal are defined in [[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]].
associated_step_blocks:
1.1 Suppose $A=LL^*$ as in [L1]. Then $A^*=LL^*=A$, so $A$ is Hermitian. For any nonzero $x$, one has $$x^*Ax=x^*LL^*x=(L^*x)^*(L^*x)=\|L^*x\|_2^2.$$ The diagonal of $L$ is positive, hence nonzero; [L2] and [L3] give $\det L
e 0$, so [L5] makes $L$ invertible and $L^*x
e 0$ when $x
e 0$. Therefore $x^*Ax>0$. [L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, algebra]
1.2 For the converse, use induction on $n$. The case $n=1$ is immediate: $A=[a]$ is Hermitian positive definite exactly when $a>0$, in which case $A=[\sqrt a][\sqrt a]^*$. [base, L1, algebra]

1.3 Assume $n>1$ and the converse for size $n-1$. Write $$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&r^*\\ r&C\end{pmatrix}.$$ Positive definiteness of $A$ at $x=e_0$ gives $a>0$. Set $\ell:=r/\sqrt a$ and $S:=C-\ell\ell^*$. For nonzero $y\in\mathbb C^{n-1}$, apply positive definiteness to $x=\binom{-a^{-1}r^*y}{y}$: $$0<x^*Ax=y^*Sy.$$ Thus $S$ is Hermitian positive definite. By the induction hypothesis, $S=\widetilde L\widetilde L^*$ with $\widetilde L$ lower triangular and positive diagonal. [ih, L1, algebra]

2.1 Define $$L:=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt a&0\\ \ell&\widetilde L\end{pmatrix}.$$ Direct multiplication gives $$LL^*=\begin{pmatrix}a&r^*\\ r&\ell\ell^*+\widetilde L\widetilde L^*\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}a&r^*\\ r&C\end{pmatrix}=A.$$ The matrix $L$ is lower triangular and its diagonal is positive real, so this is a Cholesky factorisation. [step 1.3, L1, L4, algebra]

fact_or_definition_blocks: [L1] On a nonzero finite-dimensional nil module there is a nonzero vector annihilated by all of $\mathfrak g$ ([[lem-engel-common-zero-vector]]).
associated_step_blocks: 1.3 By [L1], choose $0\neq v\in V$ with $\mathfrak g v=0$, and set $V_1=kv$. This is an invariant one-dimensional subspace annihilated by $\mathfrak g$. [L1, L2]

fact_or_definition_blocks: [L2] A nil finite-dimensional representation has a flag lowered by every represented operator ([[thm-engels-triangularization-theorem]]).
associated_step_blocks: 2.1 Conversely suppose every $\operatorname{ad}_x$ is nilpotent. The adjoint representation in [L3] is nil, so [L2] gives $0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\cdots\subset V_n=\mathfrak g$ with $[\mathfrak g,V_i]\subseteq V_{i-1}$. Induction then gives $\gamma_{r+1}(\mathfrak g)\subseteq V_{n-r}$ for $0\leq r\leq n$, and in particular $\gamma_{n+1}\subseteq V_0=0$. Hence $\mathfrak g$ is nilpotent by [L1]. [given, L1, L2, L3, algebra] ∎

fact_or_definition_blocks: [L1] Every nonzero finite-dimensional module under these hypotheses has a common eigenvector ([[thm-lies-theorem]]).
associated_step_blocks: 1.3 By [L1], choose a common eigenvector $0\neq v\in V$. Its line $V_1=kv$ is $\mathfrak g$-invariant. [L1, L2]
